text: PJSC Gazprom, a Russian majority state-owned multinational energy corporation headquartered in the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg, derives its name from the Russian phrase gazovaya promyshlennost (gas industry). In January 2022, Gazprom surpassed Sberbank to become the largest company in Russia by market capitalization. In 2023, the company reported a revenue of 8.5 trillion rubles, a significant drop from 11.7 trillion rubles in 2022. Gazprom is vertically integrated and operates in all segments of the gas industry, including exploration and production, refining, transport, distribution, marketing, and power generation. In 2018, it produced 497.6 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas and 15.9 million tonnes of gas condensate, accounting for 12% of global natural gas output. That year, Gazprom had proven reserves of 35.1 trillion cubic meters of gas and 1.6 billion tons of gas condensate. It exported gas via pipelines it builds and owns, such as Power of Siberia and TurkStream, producing 359 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas in 2018, a 13% decline from the prior year. Gazprom Neft, a subsidiary, produces about 41 million tons of oil with reserves of 2 billion tons. The company also holds stakes in finance, media, and aviation. Gazprom was established in 1989 when the Soviet Ministry of Gas Industry was converted into a corporation, becoming the first state-run corporate enterprise in the Soviet Union. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, Gazprom retained its Russian assets and secured a monopoly in the gas sector, while other national companies like Naftogaz and Turkmengaz took over assets abroad. In December 1992, following a presidential decree and government resolution, Gazprom became a joint-stock company and began distributing shares via vouchers, with 33% of shares acquired by the public by 1994 and 15% allocated to employees, while the state retained 40%, later reduced to 38%. Foreign ownership was limited to 9% until 1996, when 1% of equity was offered as Global Depository Receipts, and a $2.5 billion bond issue was launched in 1997. Under Viktor Chernomyrdin, who became Prime Minister in 1992, Gazprom evaded taxes, engaged in asset stripping, and shared assets with its executives and relatives, including the company Itera. Chernomyrdin was removed from office in 1998 and later became Gazprom's chairman. In 2000, Vladimir Putin, aiming to increase state control over key companies, replaced Chernomyrdin and Rem Viakhirev with Dmitry Medvedev and Alexei Miller, both of whom were Putin’s prior associates in Saint Petersburg. Miller and Medvedev were tasked with halting asset stripping and recovering losses, leading to Itera being denied access to Gazprom pipelines and nearly going bankrupt, with Itera eventually agreeing to return stolen assets in 2006. In April 2001, Gazprom acquired NTV, Russia’s only nationwide independent television station, from Vladimir Gusinsky’s Media-Most Holdings, after Gusinsky criticized the Kursk submarine disaster and the Second Chechen War and fled Russia. In June 2005, Gazprom subsidiaries sold a 10.7399% stake to Rosneftegaz for $7 billion, completing the sale by December 2005, which, combined with the state’s 38% share, gave the Russian government full control. The government then lifted the 20% foreign ownership cap, allowing foreign investment. In September 2005, Gazprom bought 72.633% of Sibneft for $13.01 billion, renaming it Gazprom Neft and using a $12 billion loan; the deal valued the company at £69.7 billion (US$123.2 billion) on the day of completion. In July 2006, the State Duma passed the On Gas Export law, granting Gazprom exclusive rights to export Russian natural gas. In December 2006, Gazprom signed an agreement with Royal Dutch Shell, Mitsui, and Mitsubishi to take a 50% plus one share stake in Sakhalin Energy. In June 2007, TNK-BP agreed to sell its stake in the Kovykta field to Gazprom after the Russian government questioned BP’s export rights. On 1 August 2007, Gazprom’s Sergey Kuprianov threatened Belarus with a 300% price increase on gas if debts were not paid, which was later resolved. On 23 June 2007, Russia and Italy signed a memorandum to build a 558-mile (900 km) South Stream pipeline to deliver 1.05 trillion cubic feet (30 km³) of gas annually to Europe, with a south fork to Italy and a north fork to Hungary. On 18 December 2007, Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Dmitry Medvedev signed an agreement with BASF to exploit a gas field, despite German academic warnings about overreliance on Russian gas. On 11 February 2008, Kuprianov threatened Ukraine with a gas flow halt, which was implemented in January 2009, beginning the 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas dispute. In December 2014, during a visit to Turkey, Putin announced the South Stream project would not proceed and instead committed to shipping 63 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/y) to Turkey, citing Bulgaria’s EU contract violations. In September 2012, the European Commission launched an anti-trust investigation into Gazprom, citing concerns about its dominant market position in upstream gas supply. In November 2013, Gazprom acquired Profmedia from Vladimir Potanin to expand its media interests. In May 2014, Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation signed a $400 billion contract for 38 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to China starting in 2018. Construction of the Power of Siberia pipeline began in August 2014 with pipe deliveries to Lensk, Yakutia, and gas supply to China began on 20 December 2019 as part of the energy pact; Beijing and Moscow are now negotiating a second Far Eastern gas pipeline. In June 2014, Gazprom negotiated a 24.9% stake in OMV with the Abu Dhabi-based IPIC. In July 2014, Gazprom acquired Central Partnership, one of Russia’s largest film distributors. In September 2015, Nord Stream 2 contracts were signed and the pipeline was commissioned by July 2021. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Gazprom’s export market shrank from 185 bcm in 2021 to 100 bcm in 2022 and further declined in 2023, leading to a revenue collapse and a 34% price increase in the domestic market over three years. Gazprom has also faced compensation claims for failing to supply gas under long-term contracts. In April 2025, Gazprom announced it would begin producing home appliances. In 2011, Gazprom produced 513.17 billion cubic meters of natural gas—17% of global output and 83% of Russian production—with Yamburg producing 41%, Urengoy 23.6%, Nadym 10.9%, Noyabrsk 9.3%, and others 15.2%. It also produced 32.28 million tons of oil and 12.07 million tons of gas condensate. The majority of Gazprom’s fields are in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region of Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug in Western Siberia, with the historically largest fields being Medvezhe, Urengoy, and Yamburg. After over two decades of production, these fields are in decline, with annual production dropping by 20 to 25 bcm. Production at Zaporliarnoe, Gazprom’s fourth-largest field, increased until 2004, offsetting the decline in others. Since 2004, Gazprom has maintained production by activating new smaller fields and purchasing assets from other companies. Gazprom Neft was acquired in 2005 for $13.1 billion, purchasing 75% of its shares. Gazprom’s domestic and reexport gas supply relies heavily on imports from Central Asia: 42.6 bcm from Turkmenistan, 8.5 bcm from Kazakhstan, and 9.6 bcm from Uzbekistan in 2007, with 75% of Turkmenistan’s gas exports purchased to supply Ukraine. In 2008, Gazprom paid $130/mcm to $180/mcm for Central Asian gas. In 2015, Gazprom’s proved and probable natural gas reserves were 23.705 trillion cubic meters (837.1 trillion cubic feet), a 3.8% increase from 2011, representing 18.4% of global reserves; crude oil reserves were 1.355 billion tons and gas condensate reserves were 933.3 billion tons. Of these, 59.8% of natural gas reserves (Categories A+B+C1) were in the Urals Federal District (decreasing), 20.5% in the Arctic shelf (increasing), and 8.3% in the Southern Federal District and North Caucasus Federal District. Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain supply. Nearly 37% of its reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and the Barents Sea. One of its major projects is the Blue Stream Pipeline, which delivers natural gas to Turkey via the Black Sea; the agreement was signed in 1997, the first joint was welded in 2000, and it transports 16 billion cubic meters annually. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found over 10 trillion cubic meters of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60% located in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated annual production capacity of 115 billion cubic meters (4.1 trillion cubic feet), with potential for increase.

Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain its supply. Nearly 37 percent of Gazprom's reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and in the Barents Sea. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found reserves of over 10 trillion cubic metres of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60 percent of these reserves in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated natural gas production capacity of 115 billion cubic metres per annum (4.1 trillion cubic feet per annum), with potential to increase to 140 billion cubic metres per annum (4.9 trillion cubic feet per annum). The Shtokman field, located 650 kilometres (400 mi) northeast of Murmansk and 1,000 kilometres (620 mi) west of the Yamal Peninsula in the central part of the Barents Sea, is estimated to contain up to 3.7 trillion cubic metres (130 trillion cubic feet) of gas, with potential production of 71 billion cubic metres per annum (2.5 trillion cubic feet per annum) in initial phases and up to 95 billion cubic metres per annum (3.4 trillion cubic feet per annum). Gazprom, TotalEnergies (France), and Statoil (Norway) formed Shtokman Development AG for the field's development. In 2013, in Amsterdam, Alexey Miller, chairman of Gazprom's management committee, and Jorma Ollila, chairman of Royal Dutch Shell's board, signed a memorandum outlining cooperation in Arctic shelf hydrocarbons exploration and development, in the presence of Putin and Mark Rutte. In 2008, Gazprom conducted 284.9 kilometres (177.0 mi) of explorative well drilling, 124,000 kilometres (77,000 mi) of 2D seismic, and 6,600 square kilometres (2,500 sq mi) of 3D seismic survey, resulting in a 583.4 billion cubic metre (20.60 trillion cubic feet) increase in gas reserves and a 61 million ton increase in crude oil and gas condensate reserves. Gazprom conducts prospecting in India, Pakistan, Algeria, Venezuela, Vietnam, Libya, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. Its Unified Gas Supply System (UGSS) includes 158,200 kilometres (98,300 mi) of gas trunklines and branches and 218 compressor stations with a 41.4 GW capacity, making it the world's largest gas transmission system; in 2008, it transported 714.3 billion cubic metres (25.23 trillion cubic feet) of gas, and Gazprom has claimed the UGSS has reached its capacity. Major transmission projects include Nord Stream pipelines and internal Russian pipelines. In 2021, Russia had two large LNG production plants, Yamal LNG and Sakhalin-2 LNG, both of which Gazprom has an interest in. In March 2021, the Russian Government authorized a long-term programme to develop and expand the LNG industry with nine additional LNG plants to meet the growing global LNG market. In August 2021, Russia's first LNG bunkering vessel, Dmitry Mendeleev, was completed for Gazprom. In October 2021, Gazprom and RusGazDobycha announced the construction of Baltic LNG at Ust-Luga, with access to the Baltic Sea for westward sea transportation, processing ethane-containing natural gas with a capacity of 13 million tons of LNG per year. In 2024, Gazprom faced a significant LNG tanker shortage, leading it to use the Marshal Vasilevskiy floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) for exporting LNG from its Portovaya facility, as its regular tankers like the Pskov were engaged in extended voyages to Asia, avoiding the Suez Canal and Red Sea due to Houthi attacks. In 2006, Gazprom sold 316 billion cubic metres (11.2 trillion cubic feet) to domestic customers, 162 billion cubic metres (5.7 trillion cubic feet) to Europe, and 101 billion cubic metres (3.6 trillion cubic feet) to CIS countries and the Baltic states; about 60 percent of its revenue came from European sales. In 2008, the average gas price for Russian industrial customers was $71/mcm, while households paid $54/mcm. Natural gas prices fluctuated since 2000; in late 2007, the NYMEX price was $7.53 per million Btu ($25.7/MWh), equivalent to $285 per 1,000 cubic metres, while German customers paid $250 per m3, Polish customers $290 per m3, Ukrainian customers $130 per m3, and Russian customers $49 per m3. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, due to falling export revenue, the domestic market is expected to see price increases of 34% by July 2025. Gazprom delivered gas to 25 European countries; its main export arm, Gazprom Export LLC (founded in 1973, previously known as Gazexport until November 1, 2006), holds a monopoly on gas exports to countries outside the former Soviet Union and sells most Russian gas in Europe under 25-year contracts. In late 2004, Gazprom was the sole gas supplier to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Estonia, Finland, Macedonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Slovakia, providing 97 percent of Bulgaria's gas, 89 percent of Hungary's, 86 percent of Poland's, nearly 75 percent of the Czech Republic's, 67 percent of Turkey's, 65 percent of Austria's, about 40 percent of Romania's, 36 percent of Germany's, 27 percent of Italy's, and 25 percent of France's gas. By December 2010, Italy's gas supply from Russia increased from 25 percent in 2004 to 70 percent with support from Alexander Medvedev and Antonio Fallico. In May 2006, the European Union received about 25 percent of its gas supply from Gazprom, and Gazprom entered several long-term gas contracts with European companies, with prices mainly linked to oil. In 2014, Europe accounted for 40% of Gazprom's revenue, and the proportion of gas bought in the spot market in Europe rose from 15 percent in 2008 to 44 percent in 2012. In September 2013, during the G20 summit, Gazprom signed an agreement with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to exclude the Henry Hub index from price settlements. In May 2014, Putin met with Xi Jinping and negotiated a $400 billion deal, under which Russia would supply 38 billion cubic metres annually over 30 years at $350 per thousand cubic metres starting in 2018. In 2013, the average price of Gazprom's gas in Europe was about $380 per thousand cubic metres. China offered a $50 billion loan to finance gas field development and pipeline construction to the Chinese border, with China building the remaining pipeline. In January 2023, due to sanctions following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom's gas exports fell 45% from 185 billion cubic metres (Bcm) to 101 Bcm, mainly due to the loss of the European market; in 2023, Europe purchased only 28 Bcm, the lowest level since the 1970s. In December 2025, Turkey finalized a one-year extension of its expiring gas import contracts with Russia totaling 22 Bcm; Turkish Energy Minister Bayraktar stated that supplies would continue but that the focus is on short-term contracts. On 1 January 2006, during a Russia-Ukraine gas dispute, Gazprom ceased gas supply to Ukraine and called for higher payments in line with global fuel prices; a temporary deal was reached on 3–4 January 2006. On 3 April 2006, Gazprom announced a threefold price increase for gas to Belarus after 31 December 2006; on 1 January 2007, it threatened to cut supply unless Belarus increased payments from $47 to $200 per 1,000 cubic metres or ceded control of its distribution network. Some analysts suggested the penalty was aimed at President Lukashenko for failing to pursue closer integration with Russia, while others noted Armenia paid similar prices. Gazprom requested $105, but Belarus refused; it responded that cutting supplies would deny Gazprom access to its pipelines, impairing gas transport to Europe. On 1 January 2007, a last-minute agreement was signed, with Belarus paying $100 per 1,000 cubic metres and allowing Gazprom to purchase 50 percent of Beltransgaz shares; immediately after, Belarus imposed a $42/ton transportation tax on Russian oil passing through its pipelines. On 13 March 2008, after halving gas supplies to Ukraine for three days, Gazprom agreed to supply it for the remainder of the year, removing intermediary companies. On 1 April 2014, Gazprom increased the gas price to Ukraine from $268.50 to $385.50 (£231.00) per 1,000 cubic metres; Ukraine's unpaid gas bills stood at $1.7 billion (£1.02 billion). On 30 October 2014, Russia agreed to resume gas supplies to Ukraine over winter through a deal brokered by the European Union. Gazprom is a vertically integrated company, owning its supply and distribution activities, including all main gas processing facilities in Russia, operating high-pressure pipelines, and since 2006 holding a legal export monopoly; other producers like Novatek are required to use Gazprom's facilities for processing and transport. At the end of 2008, Gazprom had 221,300 employees across subsidiaries in production, transportation, storage, and processing, with 9.5 percent in management, 22.9 percent as specialists, 63.4 percent as workers, and 4.2 percent as other employees. Gazprom's headquarters were in the Cheryomushki District, South-Western Administrative Okrug, Moscow until 2021, when they moved to the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg. Gazprom is a national champion, a concept promoted by Putin, where strategic companies serve national interests, such as selling gas domestically at prices below the global market; in 2008, Gazprom's activities accounted for 10 percent of Russia's GDP. Due to large-scale projects including Nord Stream 1 and Turkish Stream, Gazprom was a major revenue source for domestic suppliers and contractors. As of 2017, Gazprom's main shareholders were the Federal Agency for State Property Management (38.37%) and Rosneftegaz (10.97%), with Rosgazifikatsiya holding 0.89%, giving the Russian government majority control; the rest were held by investors, including 25.20% by ADR holders and 24.57% by other legal entities and individuals. Gazprom is listed on the Moscow and Karachi stock markets and is the top component of the MICEX and RTS indices; it was previously listed on London, Berlin, Frankfurt, and Singapore markets before 2022 sanctions. Gazprom has several hundred subsidiaries in Russia and abroad, directly or indirectly owned, including Gazprom International UK Ltd and Gazprom International Projects BV. Gazprom is the owner and sponsor of FC Zenit Saint Petersburg and its sports departments (basketball, volleyball), VC Zenit-Kazan, Gazprom-Ugra Surgut, and SKA St Petersburg of the KHL. On 1 January 2007, Gazprom became a sponsor of FC Schalke 04 at a cost of up to €25 million per year, extending the partnership for five years in November 2009; the sponsorship was suspended after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and was worth $150 million over five years. On 9 July 2010, Gazprom became a sponsor of Red Star Belgrade in the Serbian SuperLiga. In 2010, Gazprom was a Gold Partner of Team Katusha, alongside Itera and Rostekhnologii. On 17 July 2012, Gazprom became the official Global Energy partner of Chelsea FC for the UEFA Champions League 2012 winners, a sponsorship lasting until 2015. In September 2013, Gazprom became an official partner of FIFA tournaments from 2015 to 2018, including the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia. Gazprom was also a sponsor of the defunct Minardi F1 team in 2002–2003. In April 2021, Gazprom became a sponsor of the International Amateur Boxing Association (AIBA, now International Boxing Association) as a "general partner," a sponsorship that became controversial due to the IBA's increased Russian involvement.

On 9 July 2010, Gazprom became a sponsor of the Serbian SuperLiga football club Red Star Belgrade. In 2010, Gazprom was a Gold Partner of the Russian professional cycling team, Team Katusha, alongside Itera and Russian Technologies (Rostekhnologii). On 17 July 2012, Gazprom became the official Global Energy partner of the UEFA Champions League 2012 winners Chelsea, with the sponsorship continuing for three years until 2015. On 9 July 2012, Gazprom also became a sponsor of the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Super Cup, a partnership that lasted for three seasons until 2015 and was later extended until 2024; however, due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom's sponsorship for the Champions League and Euro 2024 was voided, ending their 10-year partnership with UEFA. In September 2013, Gazprom became an official partner of FIFA tournaments from 2015 to 2018, including the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia. Gazprom was also a sponsor for the defunct Minardi F1 team in 2002–2003. In April 2021, Gazprom became a sponsor of the International Amateur Boxing Association (AIBA, now the International Boxing Association) as a "general partner," a relationship that became controversial due to the IBA's increased Russian ties under president Umar Kremlev and ended in 2023. Gazprom is one of the world's largest greenhouse gas emitters, primarily due to methane leaks and its many gas-fired power plants. It has repeatedly been accused of using natural gas supply and pricing as a political and economic weapon against Europe and Ukraine. Donald Tusk, former prime minister of Poland, stated in April 2014 that excessive dependence on Russian energy makes Europe weak. Two boycott campaigns in Ukraine occurred in 2005 and 2013, and Russia denies weaponizing energy via Gazprom. In December 2019, Gazprom paid $2.9 billion to Ukrainian counterpart Naftogaz as ordered by a Stockholm court ruling on damage claims from alleged economic harassment. Following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom faced issues with EU countries and stated it would cut off supplies to French energy supplier Engie over failure to pay in full, a claim disputed by France's Energy Transition Minister Agnes Pannier-Runacher, who stated Russia was using gas as a weapon of war and that a complete supply interruption was a possible scenario. Yuganskneftegaz, a core production subsidiary of the Yukos Oil Company previously run by Mikhail Khodorkovsky, was targeted in 2003 when Russian tax authorities charged Yukos and Khodorkovsky with tax evasion, presenting a bill of over US$35 billion and demanding full payment on the same day. Requests for deferral, installment payments, or asset sales, including Sibneft, were rejected. Bailiffs froze Yukos' shares in Yuganskneftegaz, and on 19 November 2004, a notice was placed in Rossiyskaya Gazeta stating that Yuganskneftegaz would be sold at auction thirty days later on 19 December 2004. The auction required an advance deposit of US$1.7 billion and prior clearance by the Russian Federal Antimonopoly Service. In early December 2004, Gazprom applied through its wholly owned subsidiary Gazpromneft. On 15 December 2004, Yukos filed for bankruptcy protection in a Houston court and obtained a temporary injunction blocking Gazprom's participation. On 16 December 2004, Western banks withdrew support for Gazprom's application, and Baikalfinansgrup, a previously unknown company, submitted an application. On 19 December 2004, only Gazpromneft and Baikalfinansgrup appeared at the auction; Gazpromneft declined to offer, and Baikalfinansgrup acquired Yuganskneftegaz on its first bid. On 23 December 2004, Baikalfinansgrup was acquired by Rosneft, which later disclosed in its annual financial statement that it financed the acquisition. At the time, Sergey Bogdanchikov was the president of Rosneft and CEO of Gazpromneft. Shortly after the auction, the planned merger between Gazprom and Rosneft was abandoned, and Bogdanchikov resigned as CEO of Gazpromneft. On 7 February 2006, Vladimir Putin disclosed that Rosneft used Baikalfinansgrup as a vehicle to acquire Yuganskneftegaz to protect itself against litigation. On 22 April 2015, Gazprom was charged by the European Commission with using territorial restrictions to engage in anticompetitive behavior and imposing unfair prices, preventing gas imports at competitive prices and restricting access to high-demand areas while avoiding areas of excessive supply. Gazprom was also accused of compelling entities to consent to the now-defunct South Stream pipeline through mandatory consent clauses in long-term contracts. In 2018, Gazprom agreed to a settlement that dropped all contractual barriers to the free flow of gas in Central and Eastern European markets, granted customers explicit rights to trigger price reviews when prices diverged from competitive benchmarks, and allowed more frequent and efficient reviews. Gazprom agreed not to seek damages from its Bulgarian partners after the South Stream project ended. Had the case gone to court, it could have resulted in fines of up to $12 billion. In 2020, Gazprom agreed to reimburse Poland's PGNiG nearly $1.5 billion for years of compelling overpayment for gas supplies. In June 2021, a massive methane plume over Russia resulted from the partial shutdown of a Gazprom PJSC pipeline for emergency repair on 4 June, releasing 2.7 million cubic meters (1,830 metric tons) of methane, which has a short-term warming impact equivalent to 40,000 internal-combustion cars in the U.S. driving for a year, according to the Environmental Defense Fund. Methane's climate-warming effect is estimated to be 86 times more potent than carbon dioxide. Nord Stream is a system of offshore natural gas pipelines in Europe, running under the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany, owned and operated by Gazprom subsidiaries. The projects have been opposed by the United States, Ukraine, and other Central and Eastern European countries due to concerns over increased Russian influence and reduced transit fees. German Chancellor Olaf Scholz suspended certification of Nord Stream 2 on 22 February 2022 after Vladimir Putin recognized the Donetsk and Luhansk regions of Ukraine as independent republics. On 2 March 2022, Nord Stream 2 AG, a Gazprom subsidiary, ended business operations and laid off all 106 of its staff due to international sanctions, though earlier reports of bankruptcy were denied. On 26 September 2022, a severe drop in pressure in both NS1 and NS2 was linked to a sabotage-induced rupture in both pipes. Gazprom's Arctic oil drilling has drawn protests from environmental groups, particularly Greenpeace, which opposes drilling due to ecosystem damage and lack of safety plans. In August 2012, Greenpeace protested against the Prirazlomnaya oil platform, the world's first offshore Arctic drill site. On 18 September 2013, the Greenpeace vessel MV Arctic Sunrise staged a protest and attempted to board the Prirazlomnaya platform. After arresting two campaigners attempting to climb the rig, the Russian Coast Guard seized the ship by dropping from a helicopter and arrested thirty Greenpeace activists, towing the Arctic Sunrise to Murmansk. The Russian government intended to charge the activists with piracy and hooliganism, carrying a maximum penalty of fifteen years, but Greenpeace argued they were in international waters. The government's actions sparked global protests from governments and environmentalists. According to Phil Radford, Executive Director of Greenpeace in the U.S. at the time, the response was the "stiffest response that Greenpeace has encountered from a government since the bombing of the Rainbow Warrior in 1985." The piracy charges were dropped in October 2013, and in November 2013, 27 of the 30 activists were released on bail. In May 2014, the first shipment of Arctic oil arrived at a refinery in the Netherlands and was purchased by TotalEnergies. The episode is portrayed in the 3-hour television documentary On Thin Ice: Putin v Greenpeace. Following Russia's continued aggression toward Ukraine, the U.S. tightened debt financing restrictions on Gazprombank on 17 July 2014. On 12 September 2014, the U.S. barred U.S. persons from selling goods and services to Gazprom and Gazprom Neft related to deepwater, Arctic offshore, and shale projects. On 31 July 2014, the EU placed financial restrictions on Gazprombank, and on 8 September 2014, the EU placed financial restrictions on Gazprom Neft. In April 2018, the U.S. placed CEO Alexey Miller on the Specially Designated Nationals list, barring U.S. individuals and entities from dealing with him, with entities outside the U.S. also facing penalties if deemed to aid a sanctioned entity. Miller stated he was proud of the sanction, saying it confirmed that Gazprom was doing everything right. In December 2019, the U.S. sanctioned firms involved in the Nord Stream 2 project. On 24 February 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. expanded penalties on Nord Stream 2 AG, a Gazprom subsidiary, and sanctioned its CEO Matthias Warnig. It also expanded debt and equity prohibitions against Gazprombank, Gazprom, and Gazprom Neft. In March 2022, the European Union formally approved a ban on investments in the Russian energy sector, including Gazprom Neft. The UK banned Gazprom from its debt and equity markets on 2 March 2022, sanctioned Gazprombank on 24 March 2022, and Gazprom board members on 1 March 2023. Gazprom Energy, a UK firm, stated that it supplies 20.8% of non-domestic gas volume in Great Britain and sources gas through commodity exchanges like competitors, without depending on Russian gas supplies. In 2022, due to economic sanctions, Gazprom took the unprecedented step of suspending dividends for the first time since 1998. On 18 July 2022, during a Nord Stream 1 maintenance period, Gazprom sent a letter declaring force majeure, claiming it could not guarantee a gas supply due to extraordinary circumstances. On 26 September 2022, a rupture occurred in both Nord Stream 1 and 2 due to sabotage. In the first half of 2022, Gazprom reported high profits, roughly equal to 2021's profit, due to high prices. In the second half of 2022 and into 2023, Gazprom likely did not make a profit due to falling exports. Overall, Gazprom made a profit of 1.226 trillion roubles ($15.77 billion) in 2022, down 40% after an extra tax was levied in late 2022. On 19 December 2022, European Energy ministers agreed on a price cap of €180 per megawatt-hour for natural gas to prevent Russia from driving European prices upward. Gazprom's gas exports from Russia in 2021 were 185 billion cubic meters (Bcm), fell by 45% to 100 Bcm in 2022, and decreased again to 62 Bcm in 2023. In February 2023, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin signed an order granting Gazprom Neft the right to form its own private army. After the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the introduction of Western sanctions, Western gas companies continued to pay Gazprom Bank accounts in euros and dollars, which became blocked by sanctions. On 31 March, President Vladimir Putin signed Decree 172, requiring payments to be made by alternate means. Many Western companies refused to pay except under contract, leading Gazprom to cease supplying them. This resulted in the 2022–2023 Russia–European Union gas dispute. Arbitration cases have been initiated by several Western companies with long-term contracts for damages due to short supply or cessation of supply, including Germany's Uniper, which is claiming €11.6 billion from Gazprom, and Engie, which opened proceedings in February 2023 for short delivery. Gazprom went to arbitration for €300 million in unpaid gas from Gasum in Finland, which the arbitration ruled was payable but not in rubles. India's GAIL is also seeking compensation through a London arbitration court over Gazprom's short delivery of LNG to India, disrupted by sanctions against a Gazprom subsidiary in Germany.
